newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia seen weathering global electronics slump.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia seen weathering global electronics slump.

text.p: A global slowdown in the electronics industry muffled growth for some Malaysian manufacturers, but stopped well short of wreaking serious damage to the key economic sector, industry executives said.

In the northern island state of Penang, Malaysia's "Silicon Valley" and a manufacturing base for 80 to 90 major electronics and electrical firms, three recent major retrenchments had raised fears about the state of the sector.
A total of about 3,600 workers have been laid off in Penang, and more than 2,000 in other states.

With electronics and electrical products accounting for about half of Malaysia's total exports, any decline in the industry could spell trouble for the eight percent plus overall economic growth the country has enjoyed in the past eight years.
But analysts and government officials have said the impact on Malaysia is expected to be minimal and the industry could recover by the end of the year or in early 1997.
Firms in Penang have escaped the slump relatively unscathed, unlike the recession of 1985-86 which saw layoffs of 14,000 to 15,000 workers, industry officials said.
"These (latest workforce cuts) were more (based) on corporate decisions," K. Gopalan, manager of state-run Penang Development Corp's industry and trade division said in an interview.

He pointed out that Germany's audio products company Grundig was consolidating its marketing and production operations in Europe, and that U.S.-based personal computer firm Hewlett Packard Co had made a strategic decision to get out of the disk-drive industry worldwide.
The third firm with a major layoff in Penang, U.S. disk drive maker Quantum Storage (M) Sdn Bhd, was rebasing its operations to Japan, Gopalan said.

He noted that these and other minor layoffs by several Taiwanese manufacturers of electrical products were part of the worldwide slump in semiconductor prices and that nearly all chip makers had been suffering from oversupply.
All Penang's retrenched workers had been snapped up by labour-starved electronics and electrical firms which employ about 60 percent of Penang's labour force, he added.

Semiconductor firms operating in Penang have scaled back production in reaction to the plunge in chip prices, particularly dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips, which in June had plummeted by 70 to 80 percent of their value at the end of 1995.
Industry experts said Penang-based chip makers have reduced shifts and cut back on overtime but had not laid off staff during the slump.

Siemens Semiconductor Sdn Bhd, a unit of the German industrial giant Siemens AG, has cut back on overtime, and seen a decline of 15 to 30 percent in capacity for its products, managing director Yap Peng Hooi said in an interview.
"We were definitely affected (by the global slowdown)," he said. But he added that "we have seen some firming up now" and predicted a rebound could come by early 1997.
"There weren't any semiconductor groups that closed down (in Penang). Most pulled back a bit."
Semiconductor giant Intel Corp has the biggest corporate presence in Penang's Bayan Lepas industrial park, with six factories. It has reported no layoffs.

Chip makers form the biggest segment of electronics and electrical component manufacturers in Penang, with around 40 percent of the total output, followed by manufacturers of hard disks, audio equipment and personal computers.
